message.content:
In Texas, tenants have a number of statutory rights designed to protect them from unfair treatment and ensure safe, habitable living conditions. Below is an overview of key rights you enjoy under Texas law (Texas Property Code, Chapter 24) and related statutes: | Category | Key Rights | Practical Implications | |----------|------------|------------------------| | **Security Deposits** | • Landlord may charge up to one month’s rent for a furnished unit and two months’ rent for an unfurnished unit.
• Deposit must be returned within 30 days after lease ends, minus deductions for damages beyond normal wear & tear. | • Keep records of the condition of the unit at move‑in and move‑out. | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must maintain plumbing, heating, electrical, structural integrity, and pest control.
• Must keep the premises in a safe, sanitary condition. | • Report problems promptly; landlords must respond within a reasonable time. | | **Repair & Deduct / Rent Withholding** | • If landlord fails to repair a major defect, tenant may pay the repair cost and deduct it from rent, or withhold rent until repairs are made. | • Document all communication and keep receipts. | | **Entry Notice** | • Landlord must give at least 24 hours written notice before entering, except in emergencies. | • Keep copies of notices received. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • Tenant has the right to use the premises without interference. | • Landlord cannot harass or disturb tenants. | | **Anti‑Discrimination** | • Landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or handicap. | • File complaints with the Texas Commission on Human Rights if discrimination occurs. | | **Lease Terms** | • Lease agreements must be in writing for leases longer than one year.
• Certain terms (e.g., “no pets” clauses) are enforceable only if they comply with local ordinances. | • Review lease carefully; negotiate terms before signing. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlord must provide written notice (usually 3–30 days depending on reason).
• Eviction requires a court order; unlawful detainer actions must follow proper procedure. | • Seek legal advice if facing eviction; you may contest unlawful eviction. | | **Rent Control** | • Texas does not have statewide rent control; however, some cities may have local ordinances. | • Check local city codes for any rent limits. | | **Fair Housing** | • Tenants have the right to fair housing practices under federal Fair Housing Act and Texas law. | • Report violations to the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) or Texas Commission on Human Rights. | ### How to Protect Your Rights 1. **Document Everything** – Keep a written record of all communications with your landlord, including emails, texts, and written notices. Take photos or videos of any maintenance issues. 2. **Know the Law** – Familiarize yourself with the Texas Property Code, especially Sections 24.001–24.999. You can find the full text online at the Texas Legislature website. 3. **Use Written Notices** – When reporting problems or requesting repairs, send a written notice via certified mail or email with a read receipt. This creates a paper trail. 4. **Seek Legal Assistance** – If you believe your landlord is violating your rights, consult a tenant‑rights organization or attorney. Many nonprofits offer free or low‑cost legal aid. 5. **File Complaints** – For discrimination or harassment, file a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights or HUD. For habitability issues, you can also contact your local health department or code enforcement office. 6. **Know Your Lease** – Carefully review the lease for any clauses that might conflict with state law (e.g., “no pets” clauses that violate local ordinances). Some clauses may be unenforceable if they violate public policy. 7. **Understand Eviction Notice Requirements** – If you receive an eviction notice, verify that it complies with Texas law (e.g., correct notice period, valid reason). If it doesn’t, you may have grounds to challenge it. 8. **Consider Mediation** – Many counties offer mediation services for landlord‑tenant disputes. This can be a quicker, less expensive alternative to litigation. --- #### Quick Reference Checklist - [ ] Security deposit limit checked (max 2 months for unfurnished units). - [ ] Written notice of entry received (≥24 hrs). - [ ] Repairs requested in writing; keep receipts. - [ ] Lease agreement reviewed for compliance with Texas law. - [ ] Local ordinances checked (e.g., pet restrictions, rent limits). - [ ] Contacted local code enforcement for habitability complaints. - [ ] Filed discrimination complaint if applicable. If you have a specific situation—such as a dispute over a security deposit, a repair issue, or an eviction notice—feel free to share more details, and I can help you draft a formal letter or outline next steps.
